newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Maluf sobs, but Brazil re-election not derailed.
newsitem.headline: Maluf sobs, but Brazil re-election not derailed.

text.p: Tears were not enough for Paulo Maluf to unite the Brazilian Progressive Party (PPB) against President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's plan of a second term.

The Sao Paulo mayor's chances of shattering Cardoso's re-election dream -- and furthering his own presidential ambitions -- were fading fast after his defeat at an emotional PPB convention on Wednesday, analysts and officials said.
But the government still faces pitfalls that might scuttle a constitutional amendment that would allow Cardoso to stand again in 1998, they warned.

"The government has not put a foot wrong so far in the re-election battle, but it's not a foregone conclusion that the amendment will be approved," said Ricardo Pedreira of consultants Santafe Ideais.
The decision by the PPB to merely recommend that its members back re-election only for future presidents was widely seen as a blow to Maluf, who had hoped for a binding resolution.
He wept openly as he made an impassioned plea to delegates to back him. But newspapers said the convention's non-committal stance belied his claims to have 90 percent of the PPB's votes.

The right-wing party is crucial to the government's chances of securing the two three-fifths majorities it needs to approve the re-election amendment when it is voted on in the Chamber of Deputies, probably in January.

The PPB, combined with its Liberal Party allies, accounts for 97 of the lower house's 513 members. It normally votes with the government, but grew more hostile after the resounding win of Maluf's handpicked successor in November's municipal elections.
Nonetheless, Maluf's failure to firmly rally the PPB behind him leaves open which way the party's legislators will vote.
"Maluf's not much of a problem any more," said a government source in Congress who asked not to be named. "He had a honeymoon period after the elections, but that's fading now."
The source said the government's main concern regarding re-election was a potentially bruising contest for the presidencies of the two houses of Congress.

The two biggest powers in Congress, the Liberal Front Party (PFL) and the Brazilian Democratic Movement Party (PMDB), usually agree to alternate control of each house, but have locked horns in the run-up to February's changeover.
Should one party win both houses, the other may seek vengeance by voting against re-election, officials fear. "Things are very shaky, we can't tell what's going to happen," the source said.

The PFL, a loyal government ally, offered a ray of hope of an agreement earlier this week when its candidate for the presidency of the Chamber of Deputies, Dep Inocencio Oliveira, grudgingly dropped out of the race.

But Oliveira made it clear he would resume his candidacy, against the PMDB's equally reform-minded Michel Temer, if the PMDB did not match his gesture and allow Sen. Antonio Carlos Magalhaes to win unchallenged the Senate presidency for the PFL.
So far, however, the PMDB has shown no sign of giving up on its declared intention of running both houses.
"More than Maluf, it's the presidencies of the two houses that represent the biggest risk to re-election," said analyst Pedreira.
